short: A basic raw material or farm product, such as oil, gold or wheat, where one unit is interchangeable with another, so it trades on price.
kid: A commodity is a plain thing that is the same from every shop, like rice or sugar. One bag is just as good as another, so people only care how much it costs.
detail: A commodity is a basic good, such as crude oil, natural gas, coal, copper, gold, wheat or cotton, where one unit of a given grade is interchangeable with any other (economists call this fungible). Because the product is standard, buyers choose on price alone, so prices are set by global supply and demand and are usually quoted in US dollars. Commodities fall into energy, metals (precious and base) and agriculture, and trade both physically and through futures on exchanges such as CME, ICE and the London Metal Exchange, or MCX and NCDEX in India. They matter because they are inputs for almost everything: rising commodity prices push up inflation, squeeze manufacturers' margins and help producers. India, a large importer of oil, coal and edible oils, is especially sensitive. Common confusion: calling a product a 'commodity' in business talk means it has no brand advantage, a related but looser idea.
example: Say XYZ Ltd, a hypothetical wire maker, needs 50 tonnes of copper a month. If copper rises from $9,000 to $9,900 a tonne, its monthly metal bill goes from 50 × $9,000 = $450,000 to 50 × $9,900 = $495,000, an extra $45,000.

short: Unrefined petroleum pumped from underground, priced in US dollars per barrel and processed into fuels such as petrol, diesel and jet fuel.
kid: Crude oil is thick black juice that comes from deep underground. Big factories cook it to make the fuel that makes cars and buses go.
detail: Crude oil is unrefined petroleum pumped from underground reservoirs and processed in refineries into petrol, diesel, jet fuel, LPG, naphtha and bitumen. It is priced in US dollars per barrel (42 US gallons, about 159 litres) against benchmarks such as Brent, WTI and Dubai/Oman, with each grade trading at a premium or discount depending on its quality and location. Oil is the world's most traded commodity, and its price feeds into transport, plastics, fertilisers and inflation. India has imported more than 85 percent of the crude it uses in recent years, so higher oil prices widen the current account deficit, weaken the rupee, raise inflation and hurt airlines, paint makers and oil marketing companies, while helping upstream producers. Common confusion: a move in global crude does not pass straight to pump prices, because taxes, refining costs and pricing decisions by oil marketing companies sit in between.
example: Say a country imports 4 million barrels of crude a day. A $10 rise in the price per barrel adds 4,000,000 × $10 = $40 million a day to its import bill, or $40 million × 365 = $14.6 billion over a year.

short: The world's main crude oil price benchmark, based on light, low-sulphur oil from the North Sea and traded as futures in London.
kid: Lots of different oils come out of the ground in different places. People pick one special oil from the sea near Britain and use its price as the measuring stick for the rest.
detail: Brent is the world's main crude oil benchmark, used to price most internationally traded oil. It began with oil from the Brent field in the UK North Sea; as that field declined, the underlying basket was widened to North Sea grades such as Forties, Oseberg, Ekofisk and Troll, and in 2023 US WTI Midland crude delivered to Europe was added. Brent is light and sweet, so it is easy to refine. Headlines usually quote front-month ICE Brent futures traded in London, while physical cargoes are priced off an assessment called Dated Brent. Brent matters for India because many crudes Indian refiners buy, and the sweet-grade part of the Indian basket, are linked to it. Common confusion: Brent and WTI are both light sweet crudes but are priced in different places, so they rarely trade at the same level; Brent has usually been the higher of the two.
example: Say ICE Brent futures trade at $78 a barrel and WTI at $74. The Brent-WTI spread is $78 − $74 = $4, so a 1 million-barrel cargo priced off Brent costs 1,000,000 × $4 = $4 million more than one priced off WTI.

short: The main US crude oil price benchmark, a light, low-sulphur oil whose futures trade in New York and are delivered in Cushing, Oklahoma.
kid: This is a special oil from Texas in America. People look at how much it costs to know if oil in America is getting cheaper or dearer.
detail: West Texas Intermediate is the US crude oil benchmark: a light, low-sulphur oil whose futures contract trades on NYMEX, part of CME Group, and is settled by physical delivery at the storage hub of Cushing, Oklahoma. Because the delivery point is inland, WTI's price reflects US pipeline and storage conditions as well as global demand, and it usually trades a few dollars below Brent. WTI futures are among the most heavily traded commodity contracts, and US shale producers hedge their output with them. Physical delivery produced a famous event in April 2020, when Covid lockdowns crushed demand and Cushing's tanks neared capacity, pushing an expiring contract below zero. Common confusion: 'US crude' in headlines means WTI futures, not an average of all US oil, and that negative futures price did not mean physical oil worldwide was free.
example: On 20 April 2020 the expiring May WTI futures contract settled at minus $37.63 a barrel. Each contract covers 1,000 barrels, so a trader selling one at that price had to pay the buyer 1,000 × $37.63 = $37,630 to take the oil.

short: The benchmark price for medium-density, higher-sulphur crude from the Persian Gulf, used to price much of the oil sold to Asia, including India.
kid: Many oils come from the hot desert countries by the sea. People use oil from Dubai and Oman as the measuring stick for how much those oils cost when ships carry them to Asia.
detail: Dubai crude, usually quoted as the Dubai/Oman benchmark, is the reference price for medium sour crude from the Persian Gulf sold to Asia. The price reporting agency Platts assesses it from trading in a basket of Gulf grades, including Dubai, Oman, Upper Zakum, Al-Shaheen and Murban, because Dubai's own output is now tiny. Oman futures also trade on an exchange in Dubai. Saudi Aramco and other Gulf producers set monthly official selling prices for Asian buyers as a premium or discount to the Oman/Dubai average. Since India buys mostly sour Gulf crude, the sour-grade component of the Indian basket uses this benchmark. The Brent-Dubai spread shows the relative value of light sweet versus heavier sour oil. Common confusion: Dubai is a benchmark for a type of oil, not a sign that the oil actually comes from Dubai.
example: Say the Oman/Dubai average is $75 a barrel and a Gulf producer sets its official selling price for Asia at a $1.50 premium. An Asian refiner pays $76.50 a barrel, so a 2 million-barrel supertanker cargo costs 2,000,000 × $76.50 = $153 million.

short: Russia's main export crude oil blend, which has sold at a discount to Brent since sanctions followed the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
kid: This is oil that comes from Russia. Lots of countries stopped buying it, so Russia sells it more cheaply to the ones that still do.
detail: Urals is Russia's main export crude blend, a medium sour mix of oil from the Volga-Urals region and lighter West Siberian oil, shipped mainly from Baltic and Black Sea ports. Before 2022 it usually traded within a few dollars of Brent. After Russia invaded Ukraine, many Western buyers shunned it, the EU banned most seaborne imports and the G7 imposed a price cap, so its discount to Brent widened sharply, at times beyond $30 a barrel in 2022. India and China became the largest buyers; Russian oil went from a tiny share of India's imports before 2022 to roughly a third or more in 2023-24, lowering refiners' crude costs. The discount moves with sanctions enforcement and shipping costs. Common confusion: headline discounts are usually measured at the Russian port, so the saving on oil delivered to India is smaller once higher freight and insurance are counted.
example: Say Brent is $80 and Urals trades at a $12 discount, or $68 a barrel at the Baltic port. On a 700,000-barrel cargo the headline saving is 700,000 × $12 = $8.4 million, but if freight to India costs $3 a barrel more than for Gulf crude, the real saving falls to 700,000 × $9 = $6.3 million.

short: A weighted average of Oman/Dubai and Brent crude prices that represents the cost of oil India's refiners buy, published daily by the oil ministry.
kid: India buys many kinds of oil from many places. To get one simple number, it mixes their prices together, like taking a little from each sweet jar to fill one tasting plate.
detail: The Indian basket of crude oil is a weighted average price, published daily by the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC) of the oil ministry, that represents the crude India's refiners buy. It combines a sour-grade component, the average of Oman and Dubai prices, with a sweet-grade component, Dated Brent. The weights are reset each year in line with the sour and sweet crude processed by Indian refineries in the previous year; sour grades have carried roughly three-quarters of the weight in recent years. The government uses the basket in budget assumptions, subsidy and under-recovery calculations and, under the rules as of 2025, in the formula for domestic natural gas prices. Common confusion: the basket is a calculated index, not a grade anyone actually buys, and it does not capture discounts on Russian crude, so India's true average import cost can differ from it.
example: Say the sour-sweet weights are 75:25, the Oman/Dubai average is $76 and Dated Brent is $80. The Indian basket = 0.75 × $76 + 0.25 × $80 = $57 + $20 = $77 a barrel.
formula: Indian basket = w × (Oman/Dubai average) + (1 − w) × Dated Brent, where w is the sour-crude share of the previous year's refinery intake

short: Crude oil with little sulphur, which makes it cheaper to refine; sour crude has more sulphur. Light and heavy describe how dense the oil is.
kid: Some oil is runny and clean, and some is thick and smelly. The runny, clean kind is easier to turn into fuel, so people pay more for it.
detail: Crude oils are graded on two main qualities. Sulphur content decides sweet versus sour: sweet crude has little sulphur, roughly below 0.5 percent, while sour crude has more. Density decides light versus heavy and is measured by API gravity, a scale on which higher numbers mean lighter oil; crude above about 31 degrees is usually called light and below about 22 degrees heavy. Light sweet crudes such as Brent and WTI yield more petrol and diesel with less processing, so they normally sell at a premium. Heavy sour crudes are cheaper but need complex refineries with units such as cokers and desulphurisers, which is why highly complex Indian refineries can earn more by buying heavier, cheaper oil. Common confusion: light refers to density, not sulphur, so a crude can be light and sour, or heavy and sweet.
example: A crude with a specific gravity of 0.85 has API gravity = 141.5 / 0.85 − 131.5 ≈ 166.47 − 131.5 = 34.97, about 35 degrees, so it is light. Water, with a specific gravity of 1, scores 141.5 − 131.5 = 10 degrees, which is why very heavy crudes sit near 10.

aliases: Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries
hl: organization of the petroleum exporting countries
short: An alliance of major oil-exporting countries, led by Saudi Arabia and Russia, that agrees how much oil each member should pump.
kid: A group of countries with lots of oil sit together and agree how much to sell. If they all sell less, oil gets harder to find and costs more.
detail: OPEC, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, was founded in Baghdad in 1960 by Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela, and is based in Vienna. OPEC+ is the wider alliance formed in late 2016, when OPEC members joined about ten non-OPEC producers led by Russia to coordinate output. Together the group pumps roughly 40 percent of the world's crude. At regular meetings it sets production targets, or quotas, for each member, cutting supply to support prices or adding barrels when markets are tight. Saudi Arabia, which holds much of the world's spare capacity, is its de facto leader. Membership changes over time, as countries join or leave. For India, a big importer, OPEC+ decisions move fuel costs, inflation and the rupee. Common confusion: quotas are targets, not actual output; some members overproduce while others cannot reach their quota.
example: Say OPEC+ quotas add up to 40 million barrels a day but members actually pump 40.6 million. The 0.6 million b/d of overproduction adds 0.6 million × 30 = 18 million extra barrels to the market over a 30-day month.

short: A deliberate decision by producers, most often the OPEC+ oil exporters, to pump or mine less in order to support prices.
kid: Imagine all the lemonade stands on your street agree to make fewer cups. With fewer cups around, each cup can sell for more.
detail: A production cut is a deliberate decision by producers to pump or mine less than before, so that tighter supply supports prices. In oil the term usually refers to OPEC+ lowering members' quotas, either as a group or through voluntary cuts by a subset of countries such as Saudi Arabia and Russia. The largest ever came in April 2020, when OPEC+ agreed to remove 9.7 million barrels a day as Covid crushed demand. Miners and smelters of metals such as aluminium and nickel announce cuts too. Cuts usually lift prices in the short run but cost producers market share, and they can be offset by non-members such as US shale drillers raising output. Common confusion: a cut measured from quotas is not the same as a cut in actual supply, because some members already pump below their quota, so the real reduction can be much smaller than the headline.
example: Say OPEC+ trims quotas by 2 million barrels a day, but several members were already pumping 0.8 million b/d below their old quotas. The real reduction in supply is only 2 − 0.8 = 1.2 million b/d, or 1.2 million × 30 = 36 million barrels over a 30-day month.

short: The standard unit for measuring oil output, demand and refinery capacity: how many barrels, each about 159 litres, flow in one day.
kid: A barrel is a big drum that holds oil. Counting how many drums a country fills every day tells us how much oil it makes.
detail: Barrels per day (b/d or bpd) is the standard unit for measuring oil production, consumption, exports and refinery capacity. A barrel is 42 US gallons, about 159 litres; oil is no longer shipped in actual barrels, but the unit stuck. Large figures appear as thousand barrels a day (kb/d) or million barrels a day (mb/d). For scale, world oil demand was a little over 100 million b/d in the mid-2020s. In India, refinery capacity is usually given in million tonnes per annum (MMTPA); at roughly 7.33 barrels per tonne of crude, 1 MMTPA is about 20,000 b/d, though the exact factor depends on the oil's density. Common confusion: in some oil-industry shorthand 'M' means thousand (from Roman numerals) and 'MM' means million, so always check whether a figure is in thousands or millions.
example: A refinery rated at 10 million tonnes a year handles about 10,000,000 × 7.33 = 73.3 million barrels a year. Divided by 365 days, that is roughly 200,800 barrels a day, or about 0.2 mb/d.
formula: Barrels per day = Barrels produced in a period / Days in the period; 1 barrel = 42 US gallons ≈ 159 litres

short: Crude oil trapped in dense rock, extracted using horizontal drilling and fracking; it turned the US into the world's top oil producer.
kid: Some oil hides inside tight rocks, like juice inside a hard fruit. Workers drill sideways and squirt water very hard to crack the rock and let the oil out.
detail: Shale oil, also called tight oil, is crude trapped in dense rock layers that let oil flow too slowly for conventional wells. Producers reach it with horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing, or fracking, which pumps water, sand and chemicals at high pressure to crack the rock. The shale boom that began around 2008 in basins such as the Permian in Texas and New Mexico and the Bakken in North Dakota made the US the world's largest crude producer from 2018. Shale wells are quick to drill but their output declines steeply in the first year or two, so supply responds to prices within months. That tends to limit price spikes and weakens OPEC+'s grip on the market. Common confusion: shale oil is different from oil shale, a rock rich in kerogen that must be heated to yield oil.
example: Say a hypothetical shale well starts at 1,000 barrels a day and its output falls 65 percent in the first year. By year-end it produces 1,000 × 0.35 = 350 b/d, so the company must keep drilling new wells just to hold total output steady.

short: A weekly count of oil and gas drilling rigs at work, published by Baker Hughes, used as an early signal of future supply.
kid: A rig is a tall machine that drills deep holes to find oil. Counting how many rigs are busy each week tells us if more oil is coming soon.
detail: The rig count is the number of drilling rigs actively working at a given time. Oilfield services company Baker Hughes has published the US count weekly, on Fridays, since 1944, splitting it into rigs drilling for oil and for gas, and it also publishes international counts. Analysts watch it as an early signal of future US supply: rising prices typically bring more rigs after a lag of a few months, and new production follows months after that. Because so much US output comes from fast-moving shale drilling, the count is closely followed. Common confusion: fewer rigs does not automatically mean less oil. Each rig now drills more wells with longer horizontal sections, and producers can complete wells drilled earlier, so US output kept hitting records in 2023 and 2024 even as the rig count fell.
example: Say the US oil rig count falls from 500 to 480, down 20 rigs or 20 / 500 = 4 percent. If each rig now drills 10 percent more wells a year than before, the 480 rigs do the work of 480 × 1.10 = 528 of the old rigs, more than the 500 that were running, so drilling has actually risen.

short: The amount of crude oil held in storage; weekly US figures show whether supply is running ahead of or behind demand.
kid: Oil is kept in giant tanks, like toys kept in a toy box. If the box keeps filling up, there is plenty; if it keeps emptying, oil is getting scarce.
detail: Crude oil inventories are the stocks of crude held in tanks, pipelines and storage hubs, and they are a near real-time gauge of whether supply is running ahead of demand. The most watched data is the US Energy Information Administration's Weekly Petroleum Status Report, usually released on Wednesday and preceded by a private estimate from the American Petroleum Institute on Tuesday. Traders compare the weekly change with forecasts and also watch petrol and distillate stocks and levels at Cushing, the WTI delivery hub. OPEC+ often points to commercial stocks in rich countries relative to their five-year average. A fall in stocks, called a draw, usually supports prices; a rise, called a build, usually weighs on them. Common confusion: markets react to the surprise versus expectations, not the raw number, and a seasonal build can be perfectly normal.
example: Analysts expect a US crude draw of 2 million barrels, but the EIA reports a build of 4.5 million barrels. The surprise is 4.5 + 2 = 6.5 million barrels more oil than expected, so prices would typically fall on the news.

short: A government's emergency stockpile of crude oil, held to protect the country against supply disruptions such as wars or embargoes.
kid: A country keeps a giant hidden store of oil underground, like a snack box saved for a rainy day. It opens the box only when something goes wrong.
detail: A strategic petroleum reserve is a government-controlled stockpile of crude oil kept for supply emergencies such as wars, embargoes or natural disasters. The US created its reserve in 1975 after the 1973 Arab oil embargo; it is stored in underground salt caverns along the Gulf Coast and is one of the world's largest government emergency stocks. Net-importing members of the International Energy Agency must keep emergency oil stocks equal to at least 90 days of their net imports. India's reserve is run by Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserves Ltd (ISPRL), with caverns at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur, and more capacity planned. Governments sometimes release reserves to cool prices, as the US did on a record scale in 2022, then refill them later. Common confusion: SPR stocks are separate from commercial inventories, and a release is temporary supply that must eventually be bought back.
example: India's ISPRL caverns hold 5.33 million tonnes, roughly 5.33 million × 7.33 ≈ 39 million barrels. In 2022 the US announced a release of 1 million barrels a day for six months, about 180 million barrels in total (1 million × roughly 180 days).

short: The gap between the price of crude oil and the fuels refined from it, used as a rough gauge of refining profits.
kid: A baker buys flour and sells bread. The crack spread is the gap between what the bread sells for and what the flour cost, but for oil and fuel.
detail: A crack spread is the price difference between a barrel of crude oil and the refined products made from it, named after cracking, the refining process that breaks heavy hydrocarbons into lighter fuels. It is a market-based proxy for refining profitability. The best known is the 3-2-1 crack spread, which assumes three barrels of crude yield two barrels of petrol and one of diesel or heating oil; simpler versions track a single product, such as the diesel crack. Refiners can hedge by buying crude futures and selling product futures, locking in the spread. Wide cracks signal tight fuel supply, as in 2022, when diesel cracks soared after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Common confusion: a crack spread is a benchmark built from futures or quoted prices, not a refiner's actual margin, which depends on the crude it buys, its product mix and its running costs.
example: Crude is $75 a barrel, petrol futures $2.40 a gallon and diesel $2.70 a gallon. Converting at 42 gallons a barrel gives $100.80 and $113.40. The 3-2-1 crack = (2 × 100.80 + 113.40 − 3 × 75) / 3 = (201.60 + 113.40 − 225) / 3 = $30 a barrel.
formula: 3-2-1 crack spread per barrel = (2 × Petrol price + 1 × Diesel price − 3 × Crude price) / 3, with product prices in $ per barrel (× 42 if quoted per gallon)

short: What a refinery earns per barrel of crude: the value of the fuels it produces minus the cost of the crude and other inputs.
kid: A refinery is a big kitchen that turns oil into petrol and diesel. If the fuel sells for more than the oil cost, the kitchen keeps the extra coins.
detail: Gross refining margin (GRM) is what a refinery earns per barrel of crude processed: the value of all the products it makes minus the cost of the crude and other inputs, usually quoted in dollars per barrel. Indian refiners report GRMs every quarter, and analysts compare them with the Singapore complex margin, a widely watched regional benchmark. GRMs rise when fuel prices outrun crude, when a refinery can process cheaper heavy or discounted crude, and when it makes more high-value products such as diesel and jet fuel; more complex refineries tend to earn higher GRMs. Reported GRMs can include inventory gains or losses when crude prices move sharply. Common confusion: GRM is not profit. It comes before operating costs such as fuel, power and staff, and before depreciation and interest, so a refinery can show a positive GRM and still lose money.
example: Say XYZ Refinery, a hypothetical plant, processes 100,000 barrels in a day, sells the resulting products for $9.2 million and paid $8.4 million for the crude and other inputs. GRM = ($9.2 million − $8.4 million) / 100,000 = $8 per barrel.
formula: GRM per barrel = (Value of refined products − Cost of crude and other inputs) / Barrels of crude processed

short: A sudden, large jump or fall in oil prices, usually caused by a supply disruption, that hits inflation, growth and currencies.
kid: Imagine the sweet shop suddenly charges four times more for your favourite sweet. Everyone has less left for other treats, and that is what happens when oil gets very dear very fast.
detail: An oil price shock is a sudden, large move in oil prices, usually a spike caused by a supply disruption, that ripples through the wider economy. The 1973 Arab oil embargo roughly quadrupled prices, and the 1979 Iranian revolution doubled them again, helping cause stagflation in rich countries. Later shocks include Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait, the 2008 spike to about $147 a barrel and the jump after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. For importers like India, a shock raises inflation, widens the current account deficit and weakens the currency; the 1990 Gulf War price spike was one trigger of India's 1991 balance of payments crisis. Sharp falls, as in 2014-16 and 2020, are also called shocks and hurt exporters. Common confusion: a rise driven by strong global demand is far less damaging than one caused by lost supply.
example: Between October 1973 and January 1974 the posted price of Saudi Arabian Light crude rose from $3.01 to $11.65 a barrel, a jump of 11.65 / 3.01 ≈ 3.9 times. For an importer buying 1 million barrels a day, the daily bill rose from $3.01 million to $11.65 million.

short: A sanctions rule that lets Western firms ship, insure or finance Russian seaborne oil only if it is sold at or below a set price.
kid: Some friends agreed they would only help carry Russia's oil if it was sold cheaply. That way the oil still reaches people, but Russia earns fewer coins.
detail: The Russian oil price cap is a sanctions tool introduced by the G7, the EU and Australia in December 2022 for crude and February 2023 for refined products. It bars their firms from shipping, insuring or financing Russian seaborne oil unless it is sold at or below a set price; the original crude cap was $60 a barrel. The aim was to cut Russia's oil revenue without pulling its oil off the market and causing a price spike. Russia responded with a 'shadow fleet' of older tankers using non-Western insurance. Under the rules as of 2025, the EU and UK apply a lower cap that resets periodically below the market price, so check the live figure. Common confusion: it is not a ban on buying Russian oil or a cap on global prices; the cap itself does not stop Indian refiners buying, but deals above it cannot use Western services.
example: Under the original $60 cap, a 700,000-barrel cargo sold at $58 a barrel, worth 700,000 × $58 = $40.6 million, could use a Western insurer and tanker. Sold at $65, worth 700,000 × $65 = $45.5 million, it would have to find non-Western shipping and insurance.

short: US dollars earned by oil-exporting countries from selling crude, and the way that money is reinvested around the world.
kid: Countries that sell oil get paid in American money. They save that money or use it to buy things from other countries.
detail: Petrodollars are the US dollars that oil-exporting countries earn from selling crude, which is priced and largely paid for in dollars. Petrodollar recycling is what happens to the surplus: exporters spend it on imports or invest it abroad in US Treasury bonds and bank deposits, often through sovereign wealth funds. In the 1970s, recycled petrodollars flowed through Western banks as loans to developing countries, which fed the Latin American debt crisis of the 1980s. The arrangement, including a 1974 US-Saudi understanding on investing oil money in Treasuries, helped support the dollar's role as the main reserve currency. Moves to settle some oil trade in other currencies, such as India paying the UAE in rupees for crude in 2023, are watched as signs of change. Common confusion: there is no formal treaty requiring oil to be sold only in dollars, and no 50-year petrodollar agreement that 'expired' in 2024.
example: Say an exporter sells 2 million barrels a day at $80. It earns 2,000,000 × $80 = $160 million a day, or $160 million × 365 = $58.4 billion a year. If it spends $40 billion on imports, $18.4 billion of petrodollars is left to invest abroad.

short: A fossil fuel, mostly methane, used for electricity, heating, industry and fertilisers, moved by pipeline or shipped as liquefied gas.
kid: Natural gas is an invisible fuel that comes from underground. It makes the blue flame on some stoves and helps make electricity.
detail: Natural gas is a fossil fuel made mostly of methane, used to generate electricity, heat homes, run industry and make fertilisers such as urea; in India it also powers CNG vehicles and piped cooking gas (PNG). Because gas is costly to move, it travels by pipeline or is chilled into LNG for shipping, so prices differ by region: Henry Hub in the US, TTF in Europe and the JKM benchmark for Asian LNG. Prices are usually quoted per million British thermal units (MMBtu). Under the rules as of 2025, India sets the price of gas from older state-nominated fields as a percentage of the Indian crude basket, within a floor and ceiling. Gas has been only about 6 percent of India's energy mix in recent years, against a government target of 15 percent by 2030. Common confusion: in US news 'gas prices' often means petrol (gasoline), not natural gas.
example: Say a hypothetical fertiliser plant uses 1 million MMBtu of gas a month. At $4 per MMBtu its monthly gas bill is 1,000,000 × $4 = $4 million; if the price rises to $10, the bill becomes $10 million, an extra $6 million.

short: A pipeline hub in Louisiana whose natural gas price, set by New York futures trading, is the benchmark for US gas.
kid: Henry Hub is a place in America where lots of gas pipes meet, like a busy crossroads. The price there tells everyone how much gas costs in America.
detail: Henry Hub is a natural gas pipeline interchange in Erath, Louisiana, where many interstate and intrastate pipelines connect. It is the delivery point for the NYMEX natural gas futures contract, launched in 1990, so its price, quoted in dollars per million British thermal units (MMBtu), is the US gas benchmark. Abundant shale gas has kept Henry Hub well below European and Asian prices for most of the past 15 years. Many US LNG export contracts are priced at around 115 percent of Henry Hub plus a fixed liquefaction fee, and Indian buyers such as GAIL hold long-term US LNG contracts linked to it. Weather, storage levels and LNG export demand drive its swings, which can be violent in winter. Common confusion: a cheap Henry Hub price does not mean cheap gas in Asia, since liquefaction, shipping and regasification add several dollars per MMBtu.
example: With Henry Hub at $3 per MMBtu, an LNG contract priced at 115 percent of Henry Hub plus a $2.50 fee costs 1.15 × $3 + $2.50 = $3.45 + $2.50 = $5.95 per MMBtu at the US terminal, before shipping and regasification.
formula: Typical US LNG contract price = 1.15 × Henry Hub price + Liquefaction fee

short: Natural gas chilled into a liquid so it can be shipped by tanker across oceans and turned back into gas on arrival.
kid: If you make gas super cold, it turns into a liquid and shrinks so much it fits on a ship. Then it sails across the sea and is warmed back into gas.
detail: Liquefied natural gas (LNG) is natural gas cooled to about minus 162°C, which turns it into a liquid roughly 600 times smaller in volume, so it can be shipped across oceans in special tankers and turned back into gas at import terminals. LNG lets gas trade globally rather than only through pipelines. The US, Qatar and Australia are the largest exporters. Cargoes are sold under long-term contracts, often linked to crude prices, or on the spot market, benchmarked to JKM in Asia and TTF in Europe. In recent years India has imported roughly half of the gas it uses as LNG, through terminals such as Dahej, Hazira, Kochi and Dabhol, with Qatar its biggest supplier. Common confusion: LNG is not LPG, the propane-butane mix in Indian cooking gas cylinders, and not CNG, which is gas compressed rather than liquefied.
example: Say a long-term contract prices LNG at 12 percent of Brent (the 'slope'), with no constant. With Brent at $80, the price is 0.12 × $80 = $9.60 per MMBtu, so a cargo of 3.4 million MMBtu costs 3,400,000 × $9.60 = $32.64 million.
formula: Oil-indexed LNG price = Slope × Crude price + Constant

short: Europe's benchmark natural gas price, set at a virtual trading point in the Netherlands and quoted in euros per megawatt-hour.
kid: In Europe, gas sellers and buyers meet at one pretend marketplace in the Netherlands. The price there tells everyone in Europe how much gas costs.
detail: The Title Transfer Facility (TTF) is a virtual trading point for natural gas in the Netherlands, run by the Dutch grid operator Gasunie. Gas anywhere in the Dutch network can change hands there, and front-month TTF futures on the ICE Endex exchange have become Europe's main gas benchmark, quoted in euros per megawatt-hour (MWh). TTF drives European power and fertiliser costs and inflation, and because Europe competes with Asia for LNG cargoes, it also influences what Asian buyers, including India, pay for spot LNG. In 2022, after Russia slashed pipeline supplies, TTF briefly topped €340 per MWh in August, more than ten times its usual pre-2021 level. Common confusion: TTF is quoted in euros per MWh while Henry Hub and JKM use dollars per MMBtu, so convert units and currencies before comparing.
example: TTF at €35 per MWh equals 35 × 0.29307 ≈ €10.26 per MMBtu. At $1.10 per euro, that is 35 × 0.29307 × 1.10 ≈ $11.28 per MMBtu, almost four times a Henry Hub price of, say, $3.
formula: Price in $ per MMBtu = Price in € per MWh × 0.29307 × (US dollars per euro)

short: Coal burned in power stations and factories to make steam for electricity and heat, valued mainly by how much energy it holds.
kid: Coal is a black rock that burns very hot. Power stations burn it to boil water, and the steam spins machines that make electricity.
detail: Thermal coal, also called steam coal, is coal burned to raise steam for electricity generation and for industries such as cement. Its value depends mainly on calorific value, measured in kilocalories per kilogram, plus ash and moisture content. Seaborne benchmarks include Newcastle (Australia, high grade), Indonesian indices and API2 for delivery into Europe. India is the world's second-largest coal producer and consumer after China, and coal has generated around three-quarters of its electricity in recent years. Most supply comes from domestic mines, led by Coal India, but power plants and industries also import from Indonesia, South Africa and Australia. Prices spiked in 2022 after the war in Ukraine, squeezing Indian power producers that rely on imports. Common confusion: comparing coal by price per tonne misleads, because Indian coal has lower energy content; compare cost per unit of heat instead.
example: Coal A costs $100 a tonne at 6,000 kcal/kg, or 6 million kcal per tonne; coal B costs $75 a tonne at 4,200 kcal/kg, or 4.2 million kcal per tonne. Per million kcal, A costs 100 / 6 ≈ $16.67 and B costs 75 / 4.2 ≈ $17.86, so B is cheaper per tonne but dearer per unit of heat.
formula: Cost per million kcal = Price per tonne / (Calorific value in kcal per kg / 1,000)

short: High-quality coal that is baked into coke, the fuel used in blast furnaces to turn iron ore into iron and steel.
kid: This is a special coal that is baked to make a super-hot fuel. That fuel helps melt rocks into iron, which becomes steel for cars and bridges.
detail: Coking coal, also called metallurgical or met coal, is a higher-quality coal that is baked in ovens without air to make coke, a hard, carbon-rich fuel used in blast furnaces to turn iron ore into iron and then steel. Making a tonne of steel by the blast furnace route needs roughly three-quarters of a tonne of coal. Supply is concentrated: Australia dominates seaborne exports, and the premium hard coking coal price for Queensland cargoes is the main benchmark. India's own coking coal is high in ash, so the country imports most of what its steelmakers use, making coking coal one of the biggest cost items for Indian steel companies and a key driver of their quarterly margins. Common confusion: coking coal is not the same as coke, which is the product made from it, nor thermal coal, which is simply burned for heat.
example: Say ABC Steel, a hypothetical blast-furnace steelmaker, uses 0.75 tonnes of coking coal per tonne of steel. If coking coal rises from $220 to $260 a tonne, its coal cost per tonne of steel rises by 0.75 × $40 = $30, from $165 to $195.

short: A precious yellow metal held as jewellery, investment and central bank reserves, valued as a store of wealth in uncertain times.
kid: Gold is a shiny yellow metal that never rusts. People keep it safe because it stays precious for a very, very long time.
detail: Gold is a precious metal valued for its scarcity and durability, used for jewellery, as an investment and in central bank reserves. Global prices are quoted in US dollars per troy ounce, set by trading in London, where the LBMA Gold Price is fixed twice a day, and by COMEX futures in New York. Because gold pays no interest or dividend, it tends to fall when real interest rates and the dollar rise, and to gain in crises, which is why it is called a safe haven. Central banks, including the RBI, have been heavy buyers since 2022. India is one of the two largest consumers, alongside China, and quotes prices in rupees per 10 grams; investors can hold jewellery, coins, gold ETFs or MCX futures. Common confusion: Indian prices include import duty and GST, so they are not simply the dollar price converted at the exchange rate.
example: Say gold is $2,000 per troy ounce and $1 = ₹83. One troy ounce is 31.1035 grams, so 10 grams cost 2,000 × 83 × 10 / 31.1035 ≈ ₹53,370 before import duty and GST.
formula: Price per 10 g (₹, before duty and GST) = Price per troy ounce ($) × ₹ per $ × 10 / 31.1035

short: A precious metal used for jewellery and investment, with over half its demand coming from industry such as electronics and solar panels.
kid: Silver is a shiny grey metal that people wear as jewellery. It is also used inside phones and the sun panels on rooftops.
detail: Silver is a precious metal with a split personality: it is bought as jewellery, silverware and an investment like gold, but over half of demand comes from industry, especially electronics, solar panels and electric vehicles. Prices are quoted in US dollars per troy ounce, through London trading and COMEX futures; in India silver is quoted in rupees per kilogram and trades on MCX, and SEBI has allowed silver ETFs since late 2021. Silver's market is much smaller than gold's, so it is usually more volatile, rising faster in rallies and falling harder in sell-offs. Traders watch the gold-silver ratio to judge whether silver is cheap or dear relative to gold. Common confusion: silver is not just cheaper gold. Because so much of its demand is industrial, it can fall in a recession even when gold is rising.
example: Say gold is at $2,400 and silver at $30 an ounce; the gold-silver ratio is 2,400 / 30 = 80. At ₹83 to the dollar, one kilogram of silver (32.1507 troy ounces) is worth about 32.1507 × 30 × 83 ≈ ₹80,055 before duties and taxes.
formula: Gold-silver ratio = Gold price per ounce / Silver price per ounce

short: Rare, valuable metals, chiefly gold, silver, platinum and palladium; bullion means these metals in bars, ingots or coins valued by weight.
kid: Precious metals are rare, shiny metals like gold and silver. They are very hard to find, so people treasure them.
detail: Precious metals are rare, naturally occurring metals with high economic value, chiefly gold, silver, platinum and palladium. Bullion refers to these metals in bulk form, such as bars, ingots and coins, valued by weight and purity rather than craftsmanship. They trade in the London over-the-counter market, on COMEX in New York and, in India, on MCX and the India International Bullion Exchange (IIBX) at GIFT City, launched in 2022. Gold and, to a lesser extent, silver act as stores of value and safe havens, while platinum and palladium are mainly industrial metals used in vehicle catalysts. They differ from base metals such as copper, aluminium and zinc, which are cheaper, more plentiful and priced on the London Metal Exchange. Common confusion: precious does not mean safe; prices can swing sharply, and platinum and palladium follow car demand more than crisis fears.
example: Say an investor holds 1 kg of gold at $2,400 per troy ounce and 10 kg of silver at $30. With 32.1507 troy ounces in a kilogram, the gold is worth 32.1507 × $2,400 ≈ $77,162 and the silver 321.507 × $30 ≈ $9,645.

short: Six rare metals led by platinum and palladium, used mainly in car exhaust catalysts that cut pollution.
kid: These are rare, shiny metals that help cars breathe out cleaner air. A tiny bit sits inside the car's exhaust pipe and cleans the smoke.
detail: Platinum group metals (PGMs) are six chemically similar rare metals: platinum, palladium, rhodium, ruthenium, iridium and osmium. Most supply comes from South Africa, with Russia the other major producer, especially of palladium, so mine strikes, power shortages and sanctions can jolt prices. Their main use is in catalytic converters that clean vehicle exhaust: palladium mostly in petrol cars, platinum in diesel engines and rhodium mainly in petrol cars to cut nitrogen oxides. They are also used in jewellery, electronics, chemicals and hydrogen fuel cells. Because demand depends heavily on carmaking, the shift to battery electric vehicles, which need no catalytic converter, is the big long-term risk. Prices can be extreme: palladium traded above gold for long stretches between 2019 and 2022. Common confusion: platinum and palladium are precious metals but behave more like industrial metals than like gold.
example: Say a petrol car's catalytic converter holds 4 grams of palladium. At $1,000 per troy ounce, that metal is worth 4 / 31.1035 × $1,000 ≈ $128.60; if palladium doubles to $2,000, it is worth about $257.21.

short: The unit used to weigh precious metals, equal to 31.1035 grams, slightly heavier than an ordinary ounce.
kid: A troy ounce is a special small weight used for gold and silver. It is a little heavier than the ounce used for weighing flour.
detail: A troy ounce is the standard unit of weight for precious metals, equal to 31.1035 grams. It is about 10 percent heavier than the ordinary avoirdupois ounce of 28.35 grams used for food and post. The name is usually traced to medieval trade fairs in Troyes, France. Twelve troy ounces make a troy pound, and one kilogram equals about 32.15 troy ounces. Whenever gold, silver, platinum or palladium prices are quoted in dollars, as in '$2,000 an ounce', the ounce means a troy ounce. In India, gold is priced in rupees per 10 grams and silver per kilogram, and the traditional tola equals 11.66 grams. Common confusion: converting dollar prices using the kitchen ounce of 28.35 grams overstates the price per gram by roughly 10 percent.
example: At $2,000 per troy ounce, gold costs 2,000 / 31.1035 ≈ $64.30 per gram, or about $643 per 10 grams. Using the kitchen ounce of 28.35 grams by mistake gives 2,000 / 28.35 ≈ $70.55 per gram, overstating the price.
formula: 1 troy ounce = 31.1035 grams; Price per gram = Price per troy ounce / 31.1035
